                                      PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                     §                  OF TEXAS
STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                 §




    CIPHER DIGITAL INC. COMMENTS TO STAFF PROPOSED PROPOSAL FOR
                            PUBLICATION



        Cipher Digital Inc. appreciates the opportunity to comment on Project No. 58481,
Rulemaking Relating to the Implementation of Senate Bill 6 (89R) and PURA § 37.0561 (the
“Project”) and respectfully submits this comment letter for consideration. Cipher is proudly
committed to Texas and has made significant, long-term investments in Texas energy and
infrastructure, including developing and operating large-scale data center projects in the state.
         Cipher supports the Commission adopting durable, uniform standards that
prevent stranded transmission costs; ensure large loads meet clear technical and
reliability expectations; and require large loads to meet stringent interconnection criteria.
However, Cipher respectfully recommends the Commission revise one key feature of Staff’s
proposal because without doing so, the Project risks deterring otherwise viable and serious
development in Texas that are prepared to interconnect responsibly and contribute to the State’s
economy. Cipher’s sole comment on the Project is that the Staff should modify the proposed
$100,000 per MW “non-refundable interconnection fee” so that it is instead partially refundable
or creditable towards transmission and distribution charges based on objective milestones and
documented costs, rather than being categorically non-refundable.

        We believe this change would advance the Legislature’s direction that the Commission’s
standards be “designed to support business development in this state,” while still minimizing
stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining reliability. The Commission should design
financial commitment tools that will screen out speculation and prevent cost shifting, without
unintentionally deterring serious projects that are prepared to interconnect responsibly and
contribute to Texas’s economy.
        The Staff’s proposal indicates the standards would require large load customers to “pay a
non-refundable interconnection fee in the amount of $100,000 per MW,” in addition to posting
security for significant equipment/services, paying CIAC for direct interconnection costs, and
posting security for system upgrades. A categorical “non-refundable” treatment at this
magnitude raises several issues:
                 Legal and statutory alignment concerns. To the extent the Staff proposal’s
        $100,000/MW payment functions as a $/MW “security” or a substitute for it,
        its categorical non-refundability appears in tension with the Legislature’s refundability
        direction for $/MW security.

                Technical and cost-causation concerns. Interconnection costs vary significantly
        by location and system conditions. A submission in this docket has similarly observed
        that interconnection costs “vary dramatically” and that a “uniform, non-refundable fee
        cannot reflect these differences.” A flat, non-refundable $/MW charge risks over-
        collecting from some projects while still not precisely addressing the projects most
        likely to create stranded cost exposure.

                Consumer and economic development impacts. Even for serious projects, the
        Project increases risk in ways that are likely to chill investment decisions, slow
        contracting and site development, and potentially shift projects away from Texas; all of
        which would be contrary to the Legislature’s directive to support business
        development.

                Reliability incentives and precedent. Financial commitment is essential, but the
        best-designed commitment tools reward projects that (a) become operational, (b) meet
        load-ramp milestones, and (c) sustain operations in ways that reduce stranded cost risk.
        That approach mirrors the statutory concept that certain $/MW security should be
        refundable in whole or in part as milestones are met and operations are sustained. It is
        also broadly consistent with how interconnection regimes in other regions apply
        deposits toward actual study costs, with refund/credit mechanisms tied to work
        performed rather than being categorically non-refundable.
       A large non-refundable payment, untethered to actual costs or milestone outcomes risks
not improving reliability outcomes commensurate with its economic impact.

                                   *********************
     Recommendation. For all the above reasons, Cipher respectfully recommends the
Commission adopt either of the following two approaches:
        Option One: Modify the $100,000/MW “non-refundable interconnection fee” so that it
        becomes instead a refundable or creditable security mechanism.
                Any $/MW payment intended to demonstrate commitment should be treated
        as security that is (a) applied first to outstanding interconnection-related obligations,
        and (b) refunded, in whole or in part, based on energization and objective load ramp or
        sustained-operations milestones, and reallocation outcomes. This approach would align
        the Project with the Legislature’s refundability framework for $/MW security, while still
        preventing cost shifting and deterring speculative and problematic queue behavior.
         Option Two: Keep a limited non-refundable component, but cap it and make the
        remainder refundable or creditable as suggested in Option One.

                If the Commission concludes some portion of the fee should remain non-
        refundable for administrative process reasons, then the rule should (a) cap the non-
        refundable portion at a level reasonably related to demonstrable administrative costs
        and early-stage studies, and (b) require that the remaining balance be credited against
        CIAC or security and refundable upon energization or other milestone achievements,
        subject to offsets for costs caused by withdrawal. This approach would also better
        match the statute’s directive that unused portions of certain required payments be
        credited toward later obligations at the same site.

                                  **********************
        Cipher is committed to being a long-term Texas investor and a responsible participant in
ERCOT’s evolving large-load framework. Texas can and should adopt interconnection standards
that protect Texans from stranded costs and enhance reliability while remaining competitive for
major infrastructure investment. For the reasons above, we respectfully urge the Commission to
revise the proposed rule to make the $100,000/MW interconnection payment either fully or
partially refundable or creditable, tied to actual costs and objective milestones, rather than
categorically non-refundable, as suggested above.
       We would be happy to discuss these issues with you at any time. Feel free to contact the
undersigned by phone at (512) 963-5250 or by email at lee.bratcher@cipherdigital.com.



                                              Respectfully submitted,


                                              Lee Bratcher
                                              Head of Policy and Government Affairs
                                              Cipher Digital Inc.
